findings.claim: Five flashcard answers stop mid-sentence, including “requirements are not fully.”
findings.truth: Each flashcard answer must state the complete design-strategy point.
findings.evidence: OCR J822 section 4.2, Topic Area 1.1–1.2.

findings.claim: Four flashcard answers stop mid-sentence, including “which informs every.”
findings.truth: Each answer must complete the relevant iterative-process explanation.
findings.evidence: OCR J822 section 4.2, Topic Area 1.2.

findings.claim: Eight flashcard answers stop before their key point is complete.
findings.truth: Each answer must complete the relevant specification or evaluation explanation.
findings.evidence: OCR J822 section 4.2, Topic Areas 1.2 and 2.1.

findings.claim: Eleven flashcard answers stop mid-sentence, leaving manufacturing definitions and examples incomplete.
findings.truth: Each flashcard must give a complete, factually accurate manufacturing answer.
findings.evidence: OCR J822 section 4.2, Topic Area 2.2.

findings.claim: British Standards and UKCA are presented as universal legal requirements, and UKCA as having replaced CE marking.
findings.truth: Product rules are sector-specific. Standards are usually voluntary; UKCA and CE regimes both operate in Great Britain, and not all products need conformity marking.
findings.evidence: GOV.UK, Placing UKCA or CE marked products on the market in Great Britain, sections 3–6 (fetched 2026-09-04); OCR J822 section 4.2 Topic Area 2.3.

findings.claim: A house mark scheme states that UK Right to Repair regulations require spare parts and prevent engineered barriers to repair for a power drill.
findings.truth: Repairability duties are product- and regulation-specific; do not claim a universal right-to-repair rule for power drills.
findings.evidence: GOV.UK, Placing UKCA or CE marked products on the market in Great Britain, section 3 (sector-specific requirements); OCR J822 section 4.2 Topic Area 2.3.

findings.claim: Seven flashcard answers stop mid-sentence, including answers about UKCA and British Standards.
findings.truth: Each flashcard must give a complete answer consistent with current Great Britain conformity guidance.
findings.evidence: GOV.UK, Placing UKCA or CE marked products on the market in Great Britain, sections 3–6; OCR J822 section 4.2 Topic Area 2.3.

findings.claim: A revision tip calls orthographic drawing one of four “3D drawing types”.
findings.truth: Orthographic drawing represents an object with 2D views; the specification lists it separately from pictorial drawing types.
findings.evidence: OCR J822 section 4.2, Topic Area 3.1.

findings.claim: The lesson treats third-angle projection as universal UK practice, places the front view “centre-left”, and calls ⌀ the Greek letter phi.
findings.truth: R038 requires third-angle orthographic drawing; the front view is central in the stated layout, and ⌀ is the diameter symbol, not phi.
findings.evidence: OCR J822 section 4.2, Topic Area 3.2; direct consistency check against the lesson’s stated third-angle layout.

findings.claim: The CAD material says tolerances are applied automatically, that CAD universally enforces standards, and that STL is the direct CAD-to-CAM route.
findings.truth: Designers specify and check tolerances and conventions. STL is a surface-mesh format commonly used for 3D printing; CAD/CAM data can be used to generate CNC toolpaths.
findings.evidence: STL file format article (fetched 2026-09-04); OCR J822 section 4.2 Topic 3.3.

findings.claim: Three flashcard answers stop mid-sentence.
findings.truth: Each answer must complete the relevant digital-design explanation.
findings.evidence: OCR J822 section 4.2 Topic Area 3.3; STL file format article (fetched 2026-09-04).

findings.claim: Ranking matrices are repeatedly described as objective and as removing personal bias.
findings.truth: A weighted matrix provides structured numerical comparison, but scoring and weighting remain judgements and can introduce bias.
findings.evidence: Decision matrix article (fetched 2026-09-04); OCR J822 section 4.2 Topic Area 4.1.

findings.claim: Four flashcard answers stop mid-sentence.
findings.truth: Each answer must complete the relevant evaluation-method explanation.
findings.evidence: OCR J822 section 4.2 Topic Area 4.1.

findings.claim: The lesson says card modelling cannot test function and presents 3D-print dimensional accuracy as inherently high.
findings.truth: A card model can test simple functional features but is not suitable for structural testing or final finish. A 3D print can be used to assess dimensions and fit; accuracy depends on process and settings.
findings.evidence: OCR J822 section 4.2 Topic Area 4.2; 3D printing article (fetched 2026-09-04).

findings.claim: Six flashcard answers stop mid-sentence.
findings.truth: Each answer must complete the relevant modelling or evaluation explanation.
findings.evidence: OCR J822 section 4.2 Topic Areas 4.2–4.3.

findings.claim: All ten lesson descriptions exceed the validator's 100-character maximum.
findings.truth: Each description must be shorter than 100 characters; shorten them without changing the subject focus.
findings.evidence: Direct UTF-8 character count of raw/L01.txt through raw/L10.txt.

findings.claim: An example labels a 40 mm maximum toy-piece dimension as a “choking hazard regulation”.
findings.truth: The source needed to verify the cited toy-safety rule was not reachable. Options: replace it with a non-regulatory example, or verify the exact age-range rule and test method before using a numerical limit.
findings.evidence: UK Toys (Safety) Regulations 2011 were attempted but could not be fetched in this session.

findings.claim: The knowledge check presents repair as the universal highest-value circular-economy recovery option.
findings.truth: Recovery hierarchies use different terminology and ordering. Recommendation: ask how repair can retain product value, rather than claiming one universal top option.
findings.evidence: No single hierarchy is specified in OCR J822 section 4.2 Topic Area 2.3.

findings.claim: The lesson says all isometric lines are true length and that the drawing has no distortion.
findings.truth: The fetched source distinguishes an isometric drawing method from isometric projection, whose axes are foreshortened. Recommendation: retain the simplified classroom convention only if the distinction is explicitly taught.
findings.evidence: Isometric projection article (fetched 2026-09-04), lines 143–44.

findings.claim: Circuit-diagram symbol references “BS 3939 / IEC 60617” were not verified from a fetched source.
findings.truth: Treat the named standard references as unverified; the specification only requires circuit diagrams, not a particular named symbol standard.
findings.evidence: OCR J822 section 4.2 Topic Area 3.1; IEC source request was blocked.

summary: Ten lessons were checked. The main repair is a systematic set of incomplete flashcard answers, alongside current Great Britain conformity-marking corrections and a small number of technical-definition fixes.
